lesson.title: How Tightly the Points Cling: Strength of Association
lesson.summary: Learn to judge how tightly a scatterplot's points cluster around its overall pattern, and why a steep trend is not the same thing as a strong one.
lesson.body:
Direction tells you whether an association goes up or down, and form tells you whether the pattern is a line or a curve, but neither one tells you how reliable the pattern actually is. That is the job of strength of association: a measure of how closely the individual points cluster around the overall pattern, whether that pattern is a line or a curve. A strong association lets you predict the response variable with real confidence once you know the explanatory variable, a weak association gives you only a vague hint.

Strength is read from a scatterplot by how tightly the points hug the underlying pattern. A strong association looks like a narrow ribbon of points, all close to an imaginary line or curve running through the middle. A weak association looks like a wide, loose cloud where the general trend is barely visible through the scatter. Between those extremes sits a moderate association, with a recognizable trend but a noticeable amount of scatter around it. These are relative judgments made by eye, at least until the correlation coefficient supplies an exact number.

The study hours and exam score data, (1, 68), (2, 72), (3, 75), (4, 80), (5, 84), (6, 90), shows a strong association: every point sits close to the same upward line, and knowing a student studied for five hours lets you predict a score near 84 with real confidence. Compare that to a hypothetical data set relating shoe size to quiz score for six students, say sizes 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 paired with scores 78, 65, 90, 71, 82, 60. There is no consistent climb or fall here at all, the points scatter widely with no tight pattern, so this association, if it can even be called one, is weak to nonexistent. Shoe size gives you almost no useful information about quiz performance.

A common mistake is to confuse a steep-looking line with a strong association. Strength has nothing to do with how steep the pattern rises or falls, it has to do with how close the points sit to that pattern. A gently sloped line that every point sits almost exactly on describes a very strong association, while a dramatically steep trend surrounded by wildly scattered points describes a weak one. Always separate the question of how fast the trend rises or falls from the question of how tightly the points follow that trend, since they are answering two different things about the same scatterplot.

Judging strength by eye is a useful first pass, but it is also somewhat subjective, since two people can disagree about whether a given scatter counts as moderate or strong. The correlation coefficient, covered next, replaces that visual judgment with a precise number between -1 and 1 for any relationship with a linear form, giving strength of association the same kind of numerical backbone that the 1.5 times IQR rule gave to identifying outliers.

Strength matters practically because it tells you how much to trust a prediction. If a strong association exists between hours studied and exam score, a tutor can use study hours as a genuinely useful predictor of a student's likely score. If the association is weak, as in the shoe size example, using it to predict anything would be close to guessing, no matter how official the prediction sounds.
